thread.title: Fitbit's Plan to Conquer Apple (and the World) - Barron's

title: Fitbit's Plan to Conquer Apple (and the World) - Barron's
text:
Fitbit (FIT) Chief Financial Officer Bill Zerella was trash-talking Apple (AAPL) the other day. Bill Zerella Illustration: Bloomberg News 
“I have yet to meet anyone who owns an Apple Watch who’s passionate about the product,” he told investors at the Roth Investment Conference in Laguna Beach, Calif., adding that sales of the Apple Watch have mainly just piggybacked off sales of iPhones. 
“If you don’t have an Apple phone, you’re not buying an Apple Watch… [and] 80% of the world is Android, not Apple,” he said. 
It’s easy to laugh at this. Apple Watches are now the best-selling wearable smart device in the world, while Fitbit’s struggles have sent its stock price plunging 75% since its 2015 IPO. Falling sales and tough competition swung it from a 2015 net profit of $105 million to a 2017 net loss of $277 million. 
Last quarter, Apple Watch sales jumped 57% to 8 million, according to International Data Corporation . Fitbit unit sales fell 17% to 5.4 million. 
Yet Zerella’s anecdotal observation has a point. Ask anyone who owns an Apple Watch how they like it, and you typically get a response along the lines of, “It’s OK.” Your correspondent, too, hasn’t yet met anyone who really loves it, and it isn’t for want of asking. 
Apple doesn’t even report Watch sales, which hardly inspires confidence. According to IDC, iPhones outsold Apple Watches last quarter by 10 to 1. 
Apple did not respond to requests for comment. 
Fitbit is a company in trouble and is looking for a turnaround. At just $5.20 a share, its market value is $1.2 billion, but cash, receivables, and other liquid assets exceed total liabilities by another $626 million, so the net, or enterprise, value is $560 million. 
Compared to last year’s gross profit—before overhead—on sales of $780 million, that looks pretty cheap. On the other hand, this is a new, volatile and fluid industry and the recent trends have been down. If the company cannot get out of its current decline the stock will probably prove about $5.20 overvalued. 
So where is it headed? 
Fitbit has just launched its first fully-fledged smartwatch, the Ionic, at $299.95. Zerella said other watches at lower price points will be coming, probably this year. The company’s products run on its own operating system. “We have over 1,000 developers working on apps for Fitbit OS,” he said. “If there was another OS out there that we could leverage we would, but there isn’t.” 
But the real juice of the company’s strategy: Don’t think of us as a devices company, think of us as a health-care company. In future years more and more of the company’s revenues will come from health-care services and applications rather than from device sales, Zerella argued. 
Fitbit is teaming up with health insurers to try to change people’s behavior, drive down costs, and “potentially share some of the savings.” It is also working on products and applications to monitor and manage chronic health problems like diabetes. A scenario in which your company’s health insurance plan includes a free or nearly free Fitbit is not unimaginable. 
Fitbit’s biggest opportunity is surely that even though its own sales are under pressure, no competing product, including the Apple Watch, has really caught fire. Most competing smartwatches are big and clunky and have poor battery life.
